items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: Use of an interpreter or surrogate
items.diagnosis: Use of a qualified interpreter for a patient with limited English proficiency
items.mechanism: When a patient prefers a language other than English, a qualified interpreter supports accurate two-way communication. Basic clinician language skills, family members, and untrained staff should not substitute for a qualified interpreter for substantive medical communication.
items.vignette: A 58-year-old woman who speaks very limited English comes to a clinic visit to discuss the results of an abnormal breast biopsy and the next diagnostic steps. Her adult daughter is fluent in English and offers to interpret. The physician knows several conversational phrases in the patient's language but cannot discuss medical terminology fluently. The patient looks toward her daughter whenever the physician asks a question.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step by the physician?

options.A: Ask the daughter to interpret because she already knows the patient's medical history
options.B: Use the physician's conversational language skills and switch to English only for technical terms
options.C: Arrange for a qualified medical interpreter and speak directly to the patient through the interpreter
options.D: Give the daughter written English instructions and ask her to explain them to the patient at home
options.E: Postpone the discussion until the patient can bring a bilingual friend of her choosing

items.key_expl: A qualified interpreter should be used for substantive communication with a patient who prefers another language. The physician should continue to address the patient directly; family members, friends, or limited clinician language skills should not replace qualified interpretation.

distractor_notes.A: Family members are unqualified interpreters and can introduce errors, omissions, or filtering of sensitive information.
distractor_notes.B: AHRQ advises clinicians not to rely on basic or intermediate language skills when qualified interpretation is needed.
distractor_notes.D: Written material can supplement communication but does not replace accurate real-time interpretation of clinically important information.
distractor_notes.E: A bilingual friend is also an unqualified interpreter; delaying care to wait for one is not preferable to arranging a qualified interpreter.

items.objective: Use a qualified interpreter rather than family, friends, or limited clinician language skills when conducting substantive medical communication with a patient who prefers another language.
clues: physician has only conversational language skills

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
outline: making decisions and eliciting patient perspectives
items.diagnosis: Shared decision making when more than one medically reasonable option exists
items.mechanism: Shared decision making integrates evidence about options with the clinician's expertise and the patient's values and preferences. The clinician invites participation, compares benefits and harms, elicits what matters to the patient, and reaches a decision together.
items.vignette: A 66-year-old man with decision-making capacity has a condition for which two evidence-based treatments are medically reasonable. The treatments have similar expected efficacy but differ in adverse effects, monitoring burden, and convenience. After hearing that either option would be acceptable, he asks, ‘Which one should I choose?’ His values and preferences have not yet been discussed.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.A: Choose the treatment the physician usually prescribes because clinical experience should determine the final choice
options.B: List the two treatments and ask the patient to select one without further discussion to avoid influencing him
options.C: Ask the patient's spouse to choose because family members are less affected by the stress of illness
options.D: Recommend the treatment with the lowest direct cost without discussing other differences
options.E: Compare the benefits and harms of both options, ask what outcomes and burdens matter most to the patient, and reach a decision together

items.key_expl: Shared decision making is appropriate when multiple reasonable options exist and the tradeoffs depend on patient preferences. The clinician should explain the options and their benefits/harms, elicit the patient's values, and make the decision collaboratively.

distractor_notes.A: Clinician expertise is important, but choosing without eliciting patient values omits a core component of shared decision making.
distractor_notes.B: Merely transferring the choice to the patient without helping compare options is not shared decision making.
distractor_notes.C: A capable patient remains the decision maker; family may participate if desired but should not replace the patient's values.
distractor_notes.D: Cost can matter to patients, but automatically using it as the deciding criterion ignores other tradeoffs and the patient's preferences.

items.objective: Apply shared decision making by comparing medically reasonable options, eliciting the patient's values and preferences, and reaching a decision collaboratively.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Initial disclosure after a confirmed adverse event when the root cause is not yet known
items.mechanism: Early adverse-event disclosure should communicate known facts honestly, avoid speculation or blame, acknowledge harm with empathy/apology, explain immediate care, and establish follow-up as the investigation clarifies why the event occurred.
items.vignette: A hospitalized patient accidentally received another patient's medication and developed transient hypotension that required treatment. She is now stable. The medication error has been confirmed, but the team has not yet determined how it occurred. The attending physician is preparing for the initial conversation with the patient.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

options.A: Explain the known facts, express sincere regret, describe the current care plan, state that the cause is still being investigated, and arrange follow-up communication
options.B: Wait until the investigation is complete so that every detail can be disclosed in a single conversation
options.C: Tell the patient that a nurse probably selected the wrong medication but that the exact details are uncertain
options.D: Avoid discussing the error because the patient recovered without permanent injury
options.E: Document the event in the medical record but do not raise it unless the patient asks whether an error occurred

items.key_expl: AHRQ's CANDOR disclosure guidance supports prompt initial disclosure of an adverse event, honest explanation of what is known, no speculation, sincere apology/empathy, discussion of current care and potential consequences, and planned follow-up as more information becomes available.

distractor_notes.B: Initial disclosure should not be withheld until the full investigation is complete; disclosure is an ongoing process with follow-up.
distractor_notes.C: The clinician should explain what is known and explicitly avoid speculation or unsupported blame.
distractor_notes.D: Disclosure is appropriate after an adverse event even when lasting harm is not established; the patient should be informed of what occurred and what is being done.
distractor_notes.E: Documentation does not replace transparent communication with the patient after a confirmed adverse event.

items.objective: Disclose a confirmed adverse event promptly by communicating known facts, avoiding speculation or blame, expressing empathy/apology, addressing current care, and planning follow-up.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Communicating treatment benefit using absolute risk with a consistent denominator and time frame
items.mechanism: Risk information is easier to understand when presented as absolute frequencies with consistent denominators and a meaningful time horizon rather than relative risk alone or technical statistical notation.
items.vignette: A validated decision aid estimates that a patient's 10-year risk of a cardiovascular event is 6 in 100 without preventive therapy and 3 in 100 with therapy. The patient asks how large the expected benefit is.
items.lead: Which of the following statements best follows recommended health-numeracy communication principles?

options.B: ‘Your relative risk with treatment is 0.50 compared with no treatment.’
options.D: ‘Over 10 years, the risk goes from about 6 in 100 to 3 in 100—about 3 fewer people out of every 100.’
options.E: ‘The number needed to treat is about 33 over 10 years.’

items.key_expl: The clearest option gives absolute risk using the same denominator and the same time frame, allowing direct comparison. AHRQ specifically recommends absolute rather than relative risk and consistent denominators.

distractor_notes.A: A 50% relative reduction is mathematically correct but can exaggerate perceived benefit when presented without the corresponding absolute risk.
distractor_notes.B: A relative-risk ratio is technically correct but less directly interpretable for many patients than absolute frequencies.
distractor_notes.C: The decimal is mathematically correct but lacks an intuitive frequency representation and does not directly compare both risks.
distractor_notes.E: The NNT is mathematically consistent with a 3-per-100 absolute risk reduction, but it is a transformed summary measure rather than the recommended direct absolute-frequency comparison.

items.objective: Communicate treatment effects with absolute frequencies, a consistent denominator, and a meaningful time horizon rather than relative risk alone.

items.system: Social Sciences: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
items.diagnosis: Motivational interviewing using reflection plus an open-ended question to explore ambivalence
items.mechanism: Motivational interviewing uses patient-centered communication skills such as open-ended questions, affirmations, reflective listening, and summaries (OARS). Reflecting ambivalence and inviting the patient to elaborate supports engagement rather than confrontation or coercion.
items.vignette: A 42-year-old man who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily says, ‘I know smoking is hurting me, but it is the only thing that calms me down after work. My wife wants me to quit, but I am not sure I can.’ He is not asking for a medication recommendation.
items.lead: Which of the following is the most appropriate response by the physician?

options.A: ‘You need to quit now; continuing to smoke despite knowing the risks is irresponsible.’
options.B: ‘Smoking helps you manage stress, and you also see reasons to quit. What concerns you most about continuing to smoke?’
options.C: ‘Do you promise to stop smoking before your next visit?’
options.D: ‘I will prescribe smoking-cessation medication now so you do not have to decide whether you are ready.’
options.E: ‘If you cared enough about your family, you would find a way to quit.’

items.key_expl: The response reflects the patient's ambivalence and follows with an open-ended question, both consistent with OARS communication skills used in motivational interviewing. It explores the patient's own concerns without confrontation or coercion.

distractor_notes.A: Confrontational and judgmental language undermines the collaborative, patient-centered style of motivational interviewing.
distractor_notes.C: A closed, commitment-seeking question does not explore ambivalence or invite the patient's perspective.
distractor_notes.D: Prematurely imposing a treatment plan bypasses the patient's readiness and the communication task presented in the vignette.
distractor_notes.E: Guilt-based persuasion is judgmental and does not use reflective listening or an open-ended exploration of the patient's motivations.

items.objective: Use reflective listening and open-ended questions to explore ambivalence and elicit the patient's own motivations for behavior change.
